options.text: The audience is too broad, so people who were never going to buy are the ones doing the clicking.
The budget is too low for the platform to find buyers, so it is serving the cheapest clicks it can.
The offer is priced too high for this market, so the price needs to come down before anything else.
The page is not repeating the ad's promise, so visitors arrive thinking they have landed somewhere else.

quiz.explanation: A 2 percent CTR means the ad earned the click, so the loss happened after people landed. Start at the page stage — promise match first, then load speed and how many fields the form demands — rather than reworking the audience, budget or price that were doing their job.

quiz.prompt: Cost per sign-up has climbed from about ₱80 to about ₱140 over three weeks. Reach has held steady, conversion rate on the page is unchanged, but CTR has fallen every week. The image and copy have not changed. What is the right move?

options.text: Raise the daily budget so more people are reached and the average cost per sign-up comes back down.
Rewrite the landing page and shorten the form, then judge the change after a couple of days.
Refresh the image and opening line for the same offer and audience, then let it run a full week.
Move the campaign to a different platform, since this audience has clearly stopped responding to the offer.

quiz.explanation: Rising cost is the other numbers showing up in your wallet, and here it is the falling CTR — the likeliest read is that the audience has seen this creative often enough to stop noticing it. Change the creative only, keep everything else fixed, and give it a full week so the next reading means something.

quiz.prompt: You swapped your landing page headline yesterday. Since then the page has had 11 visits and 3 sign-ups — 27 percent, up from 12 percent. What should you conclude?

options.text: The new headline is clearly better, so roll it out to the emails and the ads today.
Nothing yet — three sign-ups is far too few to be a rate, whatever the percentage looks like.
The headline is working, so keep it and give it one more day before rolling it out elsewhere.
Restore the old headline, since a jump that large is more likely to be broken tracking than real.

quiz.explanation: Wait for enough results, not enough days. A rate built on three conversions is noise, and one day cannot show you how a full week behaves, so there is nothing here to roll out, keep or reverse yet.

quiz.prompt: You have exported two weeks of campaign data and want AI to help you read it. Which instruction is safest?

options.text: "Look at this export and explain why performance dropped in week two, and what caused each of the drops."
"Analyse this export and tell me what I should fix first, second and third, with a reason for each."
"Summarise this export, then add benchmarks for my industry so I know whether these numbers are good or bad."
"Summarise what changed between the two weeks. Describe only the numbers, and flag rates built on few results."

quiz.explanation: The model can do arithmetic on data it can see, but any "why" is a guess — you are the one who knows what you changed and when. Asking it to rank fixes or to supply industry benchmarks invites reasons and figures it has no way to check.

quiz.prompt: During your pre-publish claims check you reach a line AI drafted: "Studies show 73 percent of small businesses waste their ad budget." You cannot find any study behind it. What do you do?

options.text: Cut the number, and if the point still matters, state only the shape you have actually seen yourself.
Soften it to "studies show most small businesses waste their ad budget", which drops the specific figure.
Keep it but add "according to industry research", so it is attributed rather than stated as your own.
Ask AI for the source, then cite whatever study it returns alongside the number in the draft.

quiz.explanation: A claim with no evidence gets cut, not blurred or borrowed. Vaguer wording and an added attribution both still credit research that does not exist, and a model asked to produce a source will hand you one that sounds right and is not real.

quiz.prompt: You are publishing a review of a skincare product. The brand sent it to you free, you shortened a customer's message from three sentences to one without changing what she said, and the main product image is AI-generated. What has to be true before you publish?

options.text: Disclose the free product only, since a trimmed testimonial and a generated product image are normal practice.
Say the product was gifted, label the image as AI-generated, and keep the shortened testimonial as it is.
Restore the testimonial in full and disclose the gift, but leave the image alone since it is not a photograph.
Disclose the gift and the testimonial edit, but leave the image unlabelled since it only illustrates the post.

quiz.explanation: A gifted product is a paid partnership and has to be disclosed, and an image that could pass for a photo of the real product has to be labelled. Trimming a testimonial for length is fine as long as its meaning survives, so there is nothing to restore or flag there.

assignment.title: One campaign, start to finish
assignment.brief_mdx: Pick one real offer — your own service, a client's product, or a small business you know well — and submit a complete campaign brief as text, roughly 800 to 1,000 words. Include all seven parts: (1) a customer picture in about five lines, naming the evidence you based it on; (2) the offer on one page — what the buyer gets, price and payment terms, who it is not for, and the single action you want; (3) your voice guide as five rules; (4) the same message in three shapes: a Facebook post, an email with subject line and one ask, and a landing page outline with one call to action; (5) a two-week content calendar with dates and what goes out on each; (6) your measurement plan — the one number that defines success, the target, and what you would change if it misses; and (7) a claims check listing every claim your copy makes and the evidence behind it. At the end, say in two lines which parts AI drafted and what you changed.
criteria: The customer picture and the offer are specific and consistent, and the copy sells that offer to that person — not a vaguer version of either
One voice runs through all three pieces, and each piece is genuinely adapted to its placement rather than pasted across them
The email has a subject line and exactly one ask; the landing page outline drives one call to action and names the payment or signup step
The two-week calendar is dated, realistic for one person's hours, and every entry traces back to the campaign's offer
Success is defined by one named number with a target, plus a stated change to make if it misses — not just 'more sales'
Every claim in the copy appears in the claims check with real evidence; no invented statistics, guarantees, or undisclosed paid or AI-generated content
